newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-CRISIS DEEPENS IN THE CARIBBEAN.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-CRISIS DEEPENS IN THE CARIBBEAN.

text.p: West Indies' selectors implicitly acknowledged the current crisis in Caribbean cricket early in the New Year.
Trailing 2-1 at that stage in the five-test series, pacemen Kenny Benjamin and Nixon McLean were forced to return home with injuries.
And who did the selectors turn to? None other than Phil Simmons and Cameron Cuffy, previously discarded from the test side with good reason.
Simmons has a woeful test average of 23.80 from 24 tests while Cuffy's five test wickets at that stage had cost 190 each.

In the end, only Cuffy played in the third test, taking two for 116 in Australia's sole innings as the home side retained the Frank Worrell Trophy with a crushing innings and 183-run win in Adelaide on Tuesday.
Their selection underlined the current dearth of talent in the West Indies, with the production line that once turned out world class players in such numbers suddenly in need of a major overhaul.
The writing has been on the wall for several years now. Young men in the islands no longer eat and breath cricket as their fathers and grandfathers did before them.
Instead they have turned to sports that are faster, provide more instant excitement and, most importantly, finish in under three hours.
A drive through any parish in Barbados, the most famous cricket island in the world, provides abundant proof of the growing popularity of basketball, volleyball and soccer.

The island is now packed with flood-lit multi-purpose hardcourts which are packed each evening with strong, young men either slam-dunking a basketball or jumping to great heights to spike a volleybal.
Standing by one court was an old man who claimed to have witnessed every test match in Barbados since the mid-1930s.
With a nostalgic sigh, he said: "I saw (Wes) Hall and (Charlie) Griffith in their prime and, looking at the athletic ability I see out there, I am sure some of these boys could be great cricketers.
"But instead of playing an honourable gentleman'sz game and tearing in the 'cherry' they are out there making sport with a sissy game. All they need are skirts and it could be netball."
It is an open question whether any of the basketballers could have approached the standards of the great Barbadian fast bowlers. But there was clearly plenty of athletic talents on the court.
Asked why he preferred basketball, one youngster had a ready answer.
"It is just much more exciting and fun," he replied.

"Like most boys in Barbados, I played some cricket but the game was just too slow and there were long periods when I wasn't involved on the field. The youngsters of today need things that are happening now, we don't have the patience for a 'dead' game like cricket in thest times."

His view was reflected by several others present and while many admitted to having an interest in cricket, particularly when West Indies were doing well or playing a one-day international, none had ambitions of actually representing their country.

Even when it was pointed out that cricket now provided a very comfortable living, this did nothing to change their minds. They said cricketers earned chicken feed in comparison to players in the National Basketball Association and some even quoted salaries.
Ezra Stuart, a respected Barbadian cricket journalist, remains optimistic.
"While it is clear the youth are now a lot less intrigued by cricket and have more choices, there are still plenty of youngsters playing the game in the region," Stuart said.
"They need only to be encouraged and developed when, like all youngsters, their interest starts to drift.

"In the old days there were only two main sports, cricket and football, anbd most of the outstanding athletes then actually played both quite well. Sir Garfield Sobers played three sports for Barbados (cricket, table tennis and basketball) and Viv Richards played football for Antigua as well as cricket.
"This goes to show that it is okay to play more than one sport, but the youngsters must be encouraged to continue to play cricket and not drop it by the wayside."

Turning to the future of West Indies' cricket, Stuart conceded: "While I don't see many potential Gordon Greenidges, Brian Laras, Malcolm Marshalls and Curtly Ambroses out there, there are quite a few players with lots of promise and once they are given the chance and exposed early, West Indies can return to the top of world cricket."
In an effort to improve standards, the West Indies Cricket Board has extended its domestic first class competition to 10 matches with games being played on a home and away basis.
With just six territories playing, test contenders had only five matches to press their claim.

"With the extension of the season, which should also give the test stars time to return home from any other commitments, interest should pick up throughout the region, the young players will get a chance to rub shoulders and learn from the test players and maybe the all-conquering days of West Indies' cricket, which are not long ago, will be with us once more," Stuart concluded.
